templateText.old: I'm interested in systems where the code, documentation, and observed behavior don't quite agree. My work spans Android and iOS integrations, native code analysis, network protocols, and server-side logic. I connect research with engineering: investigate the cause, test a hypothesis, and turn the finding into a reproducible check or a focused change.
templateText.new: That's the stuff I like digging into: Android and iOS integrations, native code, network protocols, and backend logic that doesn't quite match the story. I chase the cause, put the theory on trial, and turn what holds up into a repeatable check or a focused fix.

templateText.old: Reliability is another part of that work: worker lifecycles, task queues, access control, observability, and safe updates. A successful build, a passing local test, and verified behavior in an external environment are different kinds of evidence. I aim to make clear what has been established and what remains a hypothesis.
templateText.new: I also work on the less flashy bits that keep systems from falling over: queues, worker shutdowns, access checks, logs, and safe rollouts. A green build isn't a victory lap. Neither is one passing test. I keep 'we checked this' separate from 'that's our best guess.'

contentText.old: Work on graceful shutdown, draining active operations, and safely returning unfinished tasks when a worker stops.
contentText.new: A worker shouldn't drop a mess on its way out. This work covers graceful shutdown, a bounded drain, and handing back only the unfinished tasks that worker owns.

contentText.old: Process shutdown is a normal part of a system's lifecycle. If a worker keeps accepting tasks or cannot distinguish task ownership, an update can leave work stuck or handled incorrectly.
contentText.new: Workers stop. Updates happen. The trouble starts when a worker keeps grabbing jobs or loses track of task ownership during shutdown. That's how work gets stuck or handled twice.

contentText.old: Stop accepting new work, allow active operations a bounded drain period, and conditionally update only tasks owned by that worker instance. Check repeated signals and transport failures separately.
contentText.new: Stop intake, give active work a deadline, then conditionally update only tasks owned by that worker instance. Repeated signals and transport failures get their own checks.

contentText.old: Observable shutdown behavior, regression coverage, and consistency between source code and running instances, rather than a green build alone.

textEdits.old: Two parallel lanes, physical device and emulation, each run the app with JNI and produce a native trace. Both feed one server-side verifier. Where they join, the open question is whether both belong to the same execution. No verdict is shown.
textEdits.new: Two lanes: a real device and emulation. Each runs the app through JNI and produces a native trace, then feeds a server verifier. The question at the join is whether the evidence belongs to the same run. No verdict claimed.

textEdits.old: Client sends connect with credential. Server authenticates first. On failure, the client is rejected and no connection slot is held. On success, the server registers a slot and returns an accepted, session-bound connection.
textEdits.new: The client connects with a credential. The server checks auth before claiming a connection slot. Failed check? Rejected, no slot held. Passed check? Registered and tied to the session.

A worker that knows how to quit

textEdits.old: Three states: accepting, then draining after a signal, then stopped after a deadline. Draining is bounded. On shutdown, only tasks owned by this worker instance are updated.
textEdits.new: Accepting work, then draining after a signal, then stopped at the deadline. The drain is bounded. At shutdown, only tasks owned by this exact worker get updated.

textEdits.old: Three input combinations — version A cold launch, version A resumed, version B cold launch — each map to a different observed request shape. Note: structural similarity does not equal end-to-end compatibility.

textEdits.old: API to queue to worker to external provider. The result path from worker back to the status and result endpoint passes an access check. Note at the provider: accepted does not mean delivered.

Find the layer, not a scapegoat

textEdits.old: A stack of five layers: application, HTTP, TLS, DNS, routing. An independent control request probes each layer separately. Note: one green signal does not mean a working workflow.
textEdits.new: The app, HTTP, TLS, DNS, and routing each get their own control probe. One green check doesn't prove the user's actual workflow works.
one green check ≠ a working app
